# True or false: Delivery

Branches, pipelines, reviews, migrations and releases. Small, frequent, reversible changes are the theme; check whether your habits agree.

10 statements (Foundation 5, Standard 5). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area delivery`.

### 1. Setting a team goal of 100% test coverage is a reliable way to raise quality.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A coverage goal produces tests that run code without checking anything. Treat coverage as a floor, not a target: the playbook starts at 80% line coverage on changed lines. Review the quality of the tests, not only the number.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/testing.md](../../playbook/delivery/testing.md)

</details>

### 2. Large pull requests get reviewed as carefully as small ones.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A 2,000-line pull request tends to get a quick 'looks good to me' rather than a careful read. Aim for under about 400 changed lines and split refactoring from behaviour changes. Feature flags let one feature arrive as a series of small, safe pull requests.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/code-review.md](../../playbook/delivery/code-review.md)

</details>

### 3. A GitFlow-style develop branch is a good default for a web service you deploy yourself.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Long-lived branches delay integration and hide conflicts until late. For software you run yourself, merge small changes into one protected main branch at least once a day and hide unfinished work behind flags. Keep release branches for software that customers install and run.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/source-control.md](../../playbook/delivery/source-control.md)

</details>

### 4. A pull request pipeline that takes much longer than 10 minutes makes people batch changes and skip checks.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Slow feedback pushes people to bundle work into fewer, bigger changes, and bigger changes are riskier. The playbook keeps the pull request pipeline under 10 minutes. Cache, parallelise and move slow suites after merge, and track duration weekly.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/continuous-integration.md](../../playbook/delivery/continuous-integration.md)

</details>

### 5. Retrying a failing pipeline until it goes green is a reasonable way to handle flaky tests.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A flaky test is a defect, and retries hide it while it erodes trust in every result. Quarantine a flaky test within 24 hours and fix or delete it within 14 days. Record retries so flakes stay visible.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/testing.md](../../playbook/delivery/testing.md)

</details>

### 6. Rebuilding the production image from the same tested commit can still put untested code into production.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** A rebuild can pick up a different base image or dependency version, so production may run something nobody tested. Build once and promote the tested image by its digest. Environments should differ only in size, data and configuration.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/environments.md](../../playbook/delivery/environments.md)

</details>

### 7. When several instances of an application start at once, database migrations belong in a separate pipeline step, not in application start-up.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Several instances starting at once can race on the same migration, and a slow migration blocks start-up and fails health checks. Run migrations as a separate, reviewed pipeline step before the new version starts. Destructive steps come last, after a backup check.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/database-changes.md](../../playbook/delivery/database-changes.md)

</details>

### 8. Renaming a database column and deploying the code that uses the new name in one release is safe if the deploy is quick.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** During any deploy the old version is still running, and a rollback needs the old schema. Use expand and contract: add the new column, write to both, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old column in a later release. Each step stays compatible with the version before it.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/database-changes.md](../../playbook/delivery/database-changes.md)

</details>

### 9. A breaking change is acceptable in a patch release if it fixes a bug.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Under Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, a breaking change needs a new major version, whatever the reason. A version number is a promise about compatibility. Mark breaking commits with the Conventional Commits '!' and let CI check for breaking changes.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/versioning-and-changelogs.md](../../playbook/delivery/versioning-and-changelogs.md)

</details>

### 10. Configuration and content updates need staged rollouts, just like code.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The July 2024 CrowdStrike incident came from a content update pushed to Windows hosts worldwide, not from a code release. A change that reaches every machine at once has no chance to be caught early. Roll out configuration in stages with health checks and a pause.

Read more: [playbook/delivery/gitops-and-deployment.md](../../playbook/delivery/gitops-and-deployment.md)

</details>
